outcome: I can explain why public goods are non-rivalrous and non-excludable, why the free rider problem means the market fails to provide them, and evaluate direct provision and contracting out, funded by taxes.

learn.text:
Economists sort goods with two questions. Is the good **[[rivalrous]]**: does one person's use leave less for others? Is it **[[excludable]]**: can people who do not pay be stopped from using it?

A **[[public good]]** is **non-rivalrous** and **[[non-excludable]]**. Examples: streetlights, national defence, a lighthouse. A **[[private good]]**, such as a pizza, is rivalrous and excludable. The grid also has [[club goods]] and [[common pool resources]].

Because nobody can be kept out, people can enjoy a public good without paying. This is the **[[free rider problem]]**. If people wait for others to pay, a firm cannot sell the good and make a profit. So the free market provides too little of it, or none at all. This is a [[market failure]].

The government can respond in two ways. **[[Direct provision]]**: the government makes or runs the good itself. **[[Contracting out to the private sector]]**: the government pays a private firm to do the work. Either way, **taxes** pay for it. Everyone must pay tax, so nobody can free ride.
learn.caption: The rival and excludable grid. Public goods are in the bottom right: non-rivalrous and non-excludable.

try.goal: Light up the street. Sort the goods, try to fund the lamps with your neighbours, then help the council pay for them with a tax.
try.intro:
**Level 1: Sort the goods.** A good arrives at the street. Ask two questions: is it rivalrous, and is it excludable? Then place it in the grid. Each good you sort lights the street a little more.

**Level 2: Fund the lights.** You and four neighbours each have $10 a week. Every $5 in the fund lights one lamp, and the light reaches every house, paid or not. Choose how much to give. After each week, answer a question about what happened.

**Level 3: The council decides.** Read each case. Is it direct provision or contracting out? Work out the tax per household: total cost ÷ number of households. Then judge an advantage or a disadvantage.

levels.title: Sort the goods
levels.blurb: 10 goods. Place each one in the rival and excludable grid. Get 8 right first time.

levels.title: Fund the lights
levels.blurb: 6 weeks of giving with 4 neighbours. Answer the question after each week. Get 5 right first time.

levels.title: The council decides
levels.blurb: 4 cases. Name the way, set the tax and judge it. Score 10 of 12 first-try points.

try.rivalText: Rivalrous: one person's use leaves less for others.
try.exclText: Excludable: people who do not pay can be kept out.

goods.name: Streetlights
goods.rival: When you walk under a streetlight, there is no less light for the next person. It is non-rivalrous.
goods.excl: The light shines on everyone in the street. Nobody can be kept out of it, so it is non-excludable.
goods.why: Streetlights are a public good: non-rivalrous and non-excludable. People can enjoy them without paying.

goods.name: A national defence system
goods.rival: Protecting one more person does not leave less protection for anyone else. It is non-rivalrous.
goods.excl: The army cannot protect your neighbour but leave your house out. Nobody can be kept out, so it is non-excludable.
goods.why: National defence is the classic public good. Everyone in the country is protected, paid or not.

goods.name: A pizza
goods.rival: If you eat a slice, nobody else can eat that slice. It is rivalrous.
goods.excl: The shop only gives you the pizza if you pay. It is excludable.
goods.why: A pizza is a private good: rivalrous and excludable. The market provides it well.

goods.name: A gym membership
goods.rival: One more member does not use up the gym, unless it gets very crowded. It is non-rivalrous.
goods.excl: Only people who pay can get in. It is excludable.
goods.why: A gym is a club good: excludable, but non-rivalrous until it gets crowded.

goods.name: Fish in the ocean
goods.rival: A fish caught by one boat cannot be caught by another. It is rivalrous.
goods.excl: Nobody owns the open ocean, so it is hard to stop boats from fishing. It is non-excludable.
goods.why: Ocean fish are a common pool resource: rivalrous but non-excludable. They are often overused.

goods.name: A lighthouse
goods.rival: One more ship seeing the light does not stop other ships seeing it. It is non-rivalrous.
goods.excl: A lighthouse cannot hide its light from ships that did not pay. It is non-excludable.
goods.why: A lighthouse is a public good. A private firm would find it hard to charge the ships.

goods.name: A toll road
goods.rival: One more car does not use up the road, unless there is a traffic jam. It is non-rivalrous.
goods.excl: A gate stops drivers who do not pay the toll. It is excludable.
goods.why: A toll road is a club good: drivers who do not pay are kept out, but one more car takes little away from others.

goods.name: A fireworks display in the sky over a town
goods.rival: One more person watching does not make the display smaller for anyone. It is non-rivalrous.
goods.excl: Anyone in town can look up and see it. Nobody can be kept out, so it is non-excludable.
goods.why: A fireworks display in the sky is a public good. People can watch it for free from their window.

goods.name: A T-shirt
goods.rival: While you wear the T-shirt, nobody else can wear it. It is rivalrous.
goods.excl: The shop keeps the T-shirt until you pay. It is excludable.
goods.why: A T-shirt is a private good: rivalrous and excludable.

goods.name: Grass on a village field that every farmer may use
goods.rival: Grass eaten by one farmer's cows cannot be eaten by another farmer's cows. It is rivalrous.
goods.excl: Every farmer may use the field, so nobody can be kept out. It is non-excludable.
goods.why: The shared field is a common pool resource: rivalrous but non-excludable.

weeks.prompt: Dev gave $0 this week. Does his house get the light too?

options.text: Yes. The light reaches his house anyway: nobody can keep him out of it.
options.feedback: Right. Streetlights are non-excludable. Dev enjoys the light without paying.

options.text: No. Only the houses that paid get the light.
options.feedback: Look at the street: the lamps light every house. A streetlight cannot shine only on the houses that paid.

options.text: Yes, but only half as much as the others.
options.feedback: Dev gets the same light as everyone else. The light does not depend on what you paid.

weeks.prompt: Ama, Ben and Chen all gave less this week. What is the best explanation?

options.text: They get the light anyway, so they let other people pay. This is free riding.
options.feedback: Right. When nobody can be kept out, it pays to let others fund the good. This is the free rider problem.

options.text: They do not like streetlights any more.
options.feedback: They still enjoy the light. The point is that they get it whether they pay or not.

options.text: The lamps became cheaper to run.
options.feedback: Each lamp still costs $5 a week. Nothing changed except how much people chose to give.

weeks.prompt: A new family moves into the street. Does anyone get less light?

options.text: No. One more family under the lamps takes no light away from anyone.
options.feedback: Right. Streetlights are non-rivalrous: one more user does not reduce what others get.

options.text: Yes. The light is now shared between more people, so each gets less.
options.feedback: Light is not like a pizza. One more person under a lamp does not dim it for others. It is non-rivalrous.

options.text: Yes, unless the new family pays.
options.feedback: Paying does not change how much light anyone gets. One more user does not reduce the light for others.

weeks.prompt: Each lamp costs $5 a week. It gives each of the 5 households $2 of benefit. Why does nobody want to pay for one more lamp?

options.text: For the whole street it is worth it ($10 benefit for $5). But one household pays $5 and gets only $2 back.
options.feedback: Right. The lamp is worth it to society, but not to any one payer. So each household waits for others to pay, and the lamp is not funded.

options.text: The lamp is not worth it for the street: $2 is less than $5.
options.feedback: The street gets $2 × 5 households = $10 of benefit for $5 of cost. Society wants the lamp. The problem is that one payer only gets $2 of it.

options.text: The benefit is too small to measure, so nobody can tell.
options.feedback: The numbers are clear: $10 of benefit for the street, $5 of cost. Society gains, but each payer loses.

weeks.prompt: Could a private firm sell the street its lights and make a profit?

options.text: No. It cannot stop people who do not pay from using the light, so too few people would pay.
options.feedback: Right. Non-excludability means the firm cannot charge users. Free riders mean too little revenue, so the market provides too little or none: market failure.

options.text: Yes. It could charge a price for each hour of light.
options.feedback: How would the firm collect it? The light reaches everyone, so people would free ride instead of paying.

options.text: Yes, because streetlights are rivalrous.
options.feedback: Streetlights are non-rivalrous. And the real problem for a firm is that they are non-excludable.

weeks.prompt: The council taxed every household $6. Why did the whole street light up?

options.text: Everyone had to pay, so nobody could free ride. $6 × 5 households = $30, enough for all 6 lamps.
options.feedback: Right. A tax solves the free rider problem: the cost is shared by everyone who gets the light.

options.text: The tax made the lamps cheaper to run.
options.feedback: The lamps still cost $5 each. The tax changed who pays: everyone, not just a few.

options.text: The council charged only the people who use the light.
options.feedback: The council cannot tell who uses the light, and it does not need to. Every household pays the same tax.

wayHow.direct: The government makes or runs it itself, with its own workers.
wayHow.contract: The government pays a private firm to make or run it.

wayWrong.direct: Read again: who does the work? Here the council pays a private firm. That is contracting out to the private sector.
wayWrong.contract: Read again: who does the work? Here the government's own workers do it. That is direct provision.

calcText.total: That is the total cost. Share it between the households: divide it by the number of households.
calcText.noMultiply: You divided the cost of one item. First find the total cost: number of items × cost of each.
calcText.byItems: You divided by the number of items. The tax is shared by households: divide the total cost by the number of households.
calcText.times: You multiplied by the number of households. Divide the total cost by the number of households.
calcText.other: Not yet. Tax per household = total cost ÷ number of households.

cases.title: New streetlights
cases.story: A town needs 40 new streetlights. Council workers will fit the lights and run them. Each light costs $150 a year to run. 200 households pay council tax.

options.text: The council keeps full control of where the lights go and how well they work.
options.feedback: Right. With direct provision the government decides the quality and the service, and it answers to voters for it.

options.text: The council can make a profit by charging the people who walk under the lights.
options.feedback: The lights are non-excludable, so nobody can be charged for using them. That is why taxes pay for them.

options.text: There is no opportunity cost, because taxes pay for the lights.
options.feedback: Tax money spent on lights cannot be spent on something else, such as schools. There is always an opportunity cost.

cases.title: The festival fireworks
cases.story: The town wants a fireworks display for its festival. The council pays a private events firm to run the display. The firm's price is $9,000. 450 households pay council tax.

options.text: The firm has the skills and the equipment, and firms that compete for the contract can keep the cost down.
options.feedback: Right. Contracting out can use private sector skill and efficiency, while taxes still pay for the display.

options.text: The firm can charge everyone who watches, so no tax is needed.
options.feedback: Fireworks in the sky are non-excludable. The firm cannot charge the watchers. That is why the council pays it.

options.text: The council no longer needs to check the quality of the display.
options.feedback: The council must still check that the firm does what the contract says. That is a cost of contracting out.

cases.title: The flood wall
cases.story: A town by a river needs a flood wall in 3 sections. A private building firm wins the contract to build them. Each section costs $400,000. The council pays the firm, and 4,000 households share the cost through tax.

options.text: The firm wants profit, so it may cut corners on quality unless the council checks the work.
options.feedback: Right. A firm earns more if it spends less. The council must write a clear contract and check the work, and that costs money too.

options.text: Private firms are not able to build public goods.
options.feedback: Firms can build public goods. The problem is selling them, not building them. Here the council pays, so the firm can build it.

options.text: The flood wall becomes excludable once a firm builds it.
options.feedback: The wall protects every house behind it, whoever built it. It is still non-excludable.

cases.title: The coast lighthouses
cases.story: A coast has 3 lighthouses. A government lighthouse service runs them itself, with its own staff. Each lighthouse costs $80,000 a year to run. 12,000 households pay tax to fund them.

options.text: Tax spent on lighthouses cannot be spent on other things, such as hospitals. And with no profit motive, the service may have less reason to cut costs.
options.feedback: Right. Direct provision has an opportunity cost, and a government service may be less efficient than a firm that competes for a contract.

options.text: Ships that did not pay can be kept away from the light.
options.feedback: A lighthouse is non-excludable: every ship sees the light. That is a reason for government to provide it, not a disadvantage.

options.text: Lighthouses are rivalrous, so the government should not provide them.
options.feedback: One more ship seeing the light takes nothing from others. Lighthouses are non-rivalrous.

check.prompt: What does it mean when a good is **non-excludable**?

options.text: People who do not pay cannot be stopped from using it.
options.feedback: Yes. Nobody can be kept out, so people can use it for free.

options.text: One person's use does not leave less for others.
options.feedback: That is non-rivalrous. Excludability is about whether non-payers can be kept out.

options.text: The government makes it.
options.feedback: Who makes a good does not decide whether it is excludable.

options.text: Nobody wants to use it.
options.feedback: People may want a non-excludable good a lot, for example streetlights.

hints: Think about a gate or a ticket. Can you stop people who do not pay?
A fireworks display in the sky: can you stop people from watching?
check.worked: Example: a cinema can check tickets at the door, so it is excludable. A fireworks display in the sky cannot stop anyone from watching, so it is non-excludable.
check.explanation: A good is **non-excludable** when people who do not pay cannot be stopped from using it. This leads to the free rider problem.

check.prompt: This grid sorts goods by two questions. Choose the label for each letter.

diagram.title: The rival and excludable grid
diagram.description: A grid of four boxes. The columns are rival and non-rival. The rows are excludable and non-excludable. Each box has a letter: A top left, B top right, C bottom left, D bottom right.

slots.feedback: Rival and excludable: a private good, such as a pizza.
Non-rival but excludable: a club good, such as a gym or a toll road.
Rival but non-excludable: a common pool resource, such as fish in the ocean.
Non-rival and non-excludable: a public good, such as streetlights.

hints: Read the column first (rival or not), then the row (excludable or not).
A public good is non-rival and non-excludable. A private good is the opposite.
check.worked: Example: a pizza. If you eat it, nobody else can (rival). The shop only gives it to people who pay (excludable). So it goes in the rival and excludable box: private goods.
check.explanation: Private goods: rival and excludable. Club goods: non-rival and excludable. Common pool resources: rival and non-excludable. **Public goods: non-rival and non-excludable.**

options.text: People can enjoy a good without paying for it, so too few people pay and the market provides too little of it.
options.feedback: Yes. Because non-payers cannot be kept out, each person waits for others to pay.

options.text: Buses are too cheap, so too many people use them.
options.feedback: This is not about buses. A free rider uses a good without paying for it.

options.text: Firms charge too high a price for public goods.
options.feedback: The problem is that firms cannot charge for public goods at all, so they do not provide them.

options.text: Using a good leaves less of it for others.
options.feedback: That is rivalry. The free rider problem comes from non-excludability.

hints: Who pays for a good that nobody can be kept out of?
If you get the light anyway, why would you pay for it?
check.worked: Example: a street raises money for lights. A neighbour pays nothing but still gets the light. If many people do this, there is not enough money, and the lights are not provided.
check.explanation: The **free rider problem**: people use a non-excludable good without paying. Firms cannot earn enough revenue, so the free market provides too little or none. This is market failure.

check.prompt: Why would a private firm be unlikely to build a lighthouse on its own?

options.text: It cannot stop ships that do not pay from seeing the light, so it could not earn enough revenue.
options.feedback: Yes. The lighthouse is non-excludable, so ships can free ride. The firm cannot make a profit.

options.text: Lighthouses are rivalrous, so they would run out of light.
options.feedback: One more ship seeing the light takes nothing from other ships. A lighthouse is non-rivalrous.

options.text: Ships do not get any benefit from lighthouses.
options.feedback: Ships benefit a lot: they avoid rocks. The problem is that they can benefit without paying.

options.text: Firms are not allowed to build anything near the sea.
options.feedback: The economic reason is about payment. The firm could build it but could not charge for it.

hints: Can the lighthouse choose which ships see its light?
Think about non-excludability and free riders.
check.worked: Example: a firm puts on fireworks in the sky. Anyone in town can watch from home, so few people buy tickets. The firm loses money and stops.
check.explanation: A lighthouse is **non-excludable**: every ship sees it. Ships can **free ride**, so a firm cannot earn enough revenue. The market fails to provide it, so governments usually do.

check.prompt: A town needs 50 streetlights. Each light costs $120 a year to run. 300 households share the cost equally through a council tax. What is the tax per household per year?

mistakes.feedback: That is the total cost (50 × $120). Now share it between the 300 households.
You divided the cost of one light by the households. First find the total cost: 50 × $120.
You divided the total cost by the number of lights. The tax is shared by the 300 households.
You divided the cost of one light by the number of lights. Find the total cost (50 × $120), then divide by the households.

hints: First find the total cost of all the lights.
Total cost = 50 × $120 = $6,000. Then divide by the number of households.
check.worked: Example: 10 lights cost $200 each, so the total cost is $2,000. With 100 households, the tax is $2,000 ÷ 100 = $20 each.
check.explanation: Total cost = 50 × $120 = $6,000. Tax per household = $6,000 ÷ 300 = **$20** a year.

check.prompt: A government pays a private firm to build a flood wall. Taxes pay for it. What is this called?

options.text: Contracting out to the private sector
options.feedback: Yes. A private firm does the work, and the government pays it with tax money.

options.text: Direct provision
options.feedback: In direct provision the government's own workers do the job. Here a private firm does it.

options.text: A free market
options.feedback: In a free market the firm would sell to buyers. Here the government decides and pays.

options.text: The free rider problem
options.feedback: The free rider problem is why the market fails. Contracting out is one way the government responds.

hints: Who does the work, and who pays?
The firm does the work. The government pays with taxes.
check.worked: Example: a council pays a private company to collect rubbish each week. The council decides the service and pays from taxes. This is contracting out.
check.explanation: **Contracting out** to the private sector: the government pays a private firm to provide the good, funded by taxes. In **direct provision** the government provides it itself.

check.prompt: National defence is **non-rivalrous**. What does this mean?

options.text: Protecting one more person does not reduce the protection that others get.
options.feedback: Yes. A baby born today is protected, and nobody else is less protected.

options.text: People who do not pay tax cannot be protected.
options.feedback: That is about excludability. And defence is non-excludable: everyone is protected.

options.text: Countries do not have rivals.
options.feedback: Rivalry here is about using a good, not about other countries.

options.text: Defence is free to provide.
options.feedback: Defence costs a lot. Non-rivalrous means one more user adds nothing to the cost of others' use.

hints: Rivalry asks: does one person's use leave less for others?
Think of a new family moving into the country.
check.worked: Example: a streetlight. When one more person walks under it, the light for everyone else is the same. It is non-rivalrous.
check.explanation: **Non-rivalrous**: one more user does not reduce the amount others get. National defence is non-rivalrous and non-excludable, so it is a public good.

check.prompt: Which is a **disadvantage** of contracting out, compared with direct provision?

options.text: The firm wants profit, so it may cut quality unless the government checks its work.
options.feedback: Yes. The government must write a clear contract and check the work, and that costs money too.

options.text: The good becomes excludable, so people must pay to use it.
options.feedback: Who builds a streetlight does not change whether it is excludable. People still use it for free.

options.text: Taxes are not needed any more.
options.feedback: The government still pays the firm, so taxes are still needed.

options.text: Private firms always cost more than the government.
options.feedback: Competition for the contract can make firms cheaper. That is an advantage of contracting out.

hints: What does a private firm want?
What could happen to quality if nobody checks?
check.worked: Example: a council pays a firm to clean the streets. To cut costs, the firm cleans less often. The council must check the work and can fine the firm.
check.explanation: Contracting out can use firms' skills and **competition** to keep costs down. But a firm's **profit motive** may lead it to cut quality, so the government must monitor the contract.

check.prompt: Five households share a street. The lights cost $30 a week. Two households refuse to pay, but they still get the light. The other three share the full cost equally. How much does each of the three pay?

mistakes.feedback: $6 is what each would pay if all five paid. Only three households are paying.
You divided by the two households who refuse. The cost is shared by the three who pay.
That is the full cost. Share it between the three households who pay.

hints: Only the households who pay share the cost.
check.worked: Example: a party costs $40 for four friends, but one friend refuses to pay. The other three pay $40 ÷ 3 = $13.33 each, not $10.
check.explanation: $30 ÷ 3 = **$10** each, instead of $6 if all five paid. Free riders push the cost onto others, so the payers may stop paying too. A tax makes everyone pay.

explain.prompt: Explain why the households on your street could not fund all 6 streetlights by giving money. Then evaluate direct provision of the town's 40 new streetlights, paid for by council tax.
explain.facts:
- Your street has **5 households**: you, Ama, Ben, Chen and Dev. Each has **$10** a week.
- The street has **6 lamps**. Each lamp costs **$5** a week, so all 6 lamps cost **$30** a week.
- The light reaches every house, paid or not.
- One lit lamp gives each household **$2** of benefit a week, so it is worth **$10** to the whole street.
- Dev always gave $0, and the others gave less each week. Even if you gave all $10, the street never raised the $30 it needed.

teacherNotes: Level 1 sorts ten goods into the rival and excludable grid. Club goods are not named in the 2.9 guide, but the grid needs all four boxes; common pool resources link back to 2.8. Level 2 is a public goods game with fixed computer neighbours: Dev always free rides and the others give less each week, so voluntary giving can never light all six lamps, even if the student gives everything. Each lamp is worth $10 to the street but costs one payer $5 for a $2 benefit: ask students why the rational choice for each household is bad for the street. The last week shows the council tax. Level 3 covers both government responses in the guide: direct provision and contracting out to the private sector, funded by taxes. There are no HL parts in 2.9. Discussion idea: should a town contract out its streetlights? Who gains and who could lose?
